posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring compliance pain post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the 'explainability' problem as the real blocker, not AI itself, to position credibility naturally
posts.draft_comment: The ban wasn't really about ChatGPT — it was about not being able to reconstruct the reasoning. That's the bit most AI tools completely skip over. A number without a trail is just a guess with good formatting. I'm curious whether your team would trust AI outputs again if every figure came with a full audit trail, or has that ship sailed?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with Power BI adoption failure — validate the pain with a specific insight about trust vs. tooling, don't pitch
posts.draft_comment: The 18 months wasn't wasted on the dashboard — it was spent learning that adoption is a trust problem, not a technology problem. Finance teams have been burned by numbers that looked right but weren't, so they default to the spreadsheet they can trace with their own hands. The question I keep hearing isn't 'can we build it' but 'whose job is it to make people believe it?'

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post about dashboard overload — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'decision proximity' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is basically a confession that nobody knows what actually matters. The jump to 85% usage tells you everything — people don't avoid dashboards because they're lazy, they avoid them because most dashboards don't connect to anything they can actually do tomorrow. The real question isn't how many metrics you cut, it's whether the ones you kept make the next decision obvious.

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging with a post about BI chaos — validate the 'who owns truth' framing, add the insight that the problem is semantic not technical
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so recognisable. The tool was never the problem — it's that five teams built their own version of revenue because nobody sat down and agreed what revenue actually meant before anyone opened a laptop. Power BI, Tableau, whatever — they're all just very fast ways to scale a disagreement. Who owned the definition before the dashboards got built?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO raising AI hallucinations as a material risk with a CEO ICP prospect engaging — validate the security framing, add the trust layer insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is right and I don't think the industry has caught up to it yet. Most teams are still treating hallucinated outputs as a QA problem — something to catch before the report goes out. But if someone acts on a number before it gets caught, the damage is already done. The question isn't just 'is this accurate' — it's 'who's accountable when it isn't?'

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: CEO at 65-person advisory firm calling out the self-service BI lie, with a COO ICP engaging — validate the pain with a specific observation about where the breakdown actually happens
posts.draft_comment: The '£200k and one user' story is so common it's basically a BI industry cliché at this point. The problem isn't that people can't learn tools — it's that most BI platforms were designed to impress a procurement committee, not help a sales director answer a question on a Tuesday morning. Complexity gets built in because it signals value to the buyer, not the user. Wonder if that ever gets fixed while the people selling and the people using are never the same person.

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a likely ICP company calling out data trust issues — validate the culture diagnosis and add a sharper observation about why the filter problem is actually a governance problem nobody owns
posts.draft_comment: The filter thing is almost always a symptom of the same root cause — nobody agreed on what the numbers *mean* before they built the dashboard. Culture matters, but in my experience it's less about attitudes and more about the fact that there's no single person whose job it is to say 'this is the definition, full stop.' Three teams applying three filters usually means three teams who were never in the same room when the metric was defined. Who owned that conversation at Oakwood?

posts.post_text: Enterprise analytics teams are wasting 40% of their time on ad-hoc reporting requests. Our new AI-Powered Analytics eliminates the bottleneck entirely. See how Fortune 500 companies are scaling their data teams with ThoughtSpot. #analytics #enterprise
posts.angle: ThoughtSpot pushing 'eliminate the bottleneck entirely' enterprise narrative — challenge the assumption that AI removes the problem vs. just relocating it
posts.draft_comment: 40% on ad-hoc requests is real, but I'd push back on 'eliminates the bottleneck entirely.' In my experience the bottleneck just moves — from pulling the report to arguing about why the AI's number doesn't match what finance has. Wonder how many of those Fortune 500 teams are measuring trust in the output, not just speed of delivery?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing a real adoption failure with enterprise AI — validate the 'nobody knows what to ask' root cause and reframe it as a data literacy problem, not a tool problem
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is brutal but honestly not surprising. 'Nobody knows what to ask' is the whole ballgame — if people don't have a clear mental model of what their data even contains, a smarter prompt box doesn't fix that. Shadow AI on personal phones is just people voting with their feet for something that feels less like homework. Curious whether the 88% who aren't using it could even articulate what question they'd want answered first.
